issues.detail: Missing error scenarios (ClickHouse unavailability, event loss on service restart), edge cases (schema evolution, connection pooling), and operational aspects (monitoring, authentication, scaling).

Dashboard API and Docker Compose setup guidance lack concrete code examples; schema and ingestion service are fully runnable, but dashboard wiring and containerization require significant additional implementation.

scenarios.name: saas-events-schema
scenarios.rationale: Response B explicitly satisfies all 5 rubric requirements (MergeTree, LowCardinality on low-cardinality strings, all base fields with correct types/names, TTL 180 days, ORDER BY event_name primary), while Response A omits LowCardinality entirely, uses wrong field names (event_type vs event_name), DateTime instead of DateTime64(3), missing device_type, and puts event_date before event_name in ORDER BY—critical misses despite more elaborate content.

scenarios.name: ingestion-service-with-buffers
scenarios.rationale: Response A comprehensively covers all rubric requirements: validates event_name/timestamp, accepts JSON arrays, implements 3 retries with proper exponential backoff (500ms→1s), writes dead-letter files, and includes last_flush in health. Response B fails on critical requirements: no input validation, no array support, retries only once with fixed delay (not exponential), no dead-letter file, and health endpoint omits last_flush timestamp.

scenarios.name: dashboard-queries-time-range
scenarios.rationale: Response A fully implements the rubric: uses uniq() for active users, count(DISTINCT) for top features, countIf() for funnels, all time ranges with query parameters, and 5-second caching. Response B uses PostgreSQL with COUNT(DISTINCT) and SUM(CASE) instead of the required uniq() and countIf() functions (ClickHouse-specific), and sets cache TTLs to 1-60 minutes instead of 3-5 seconds, failing three critical rubric requirements.
